items.title: Bill Huntington Interview, 1961-12-27
items.q: Then I began to listen to, to, uh, I guess Teddy Wilson and Coleman Hawkins and people of that sort.

ctx.x: Sure. Yeah, just talk. Just say anything that comes to your mind. No, I'd rather not do that. . .

Well, uh, when I was about fifteen, uh, uh, actually through the efforts of Alvin Purnell. You see, I used to sit in with George Lewis and Alvin Purnell had a thing going where he'd play passing chords. And, uh, I was told when I was a kid that I had some kind of fantastic gear. I was some kind of child prodigy or something, you see. And so, uh, I'd hear all the things he was playing. And I'd tell Lawrence, why aren't you playing the same chords Alton's playing? You know, they sound like they're fitting more into…
Who did you like when you started playing? You mentioned Bonk, and then there must have been some other musicians. You said you met a lot on the mind.

items.title: Bill Huntington and Charlie Suhor Interview, 1992-04-06
items.q: had played jazz with people like Coleman Hawkins

ctx.x: Well, we used to play and Herb Tasson used to come and jam with us at the, at the Premiers Fountain Lounge Club. And a lot of people used to hang around there, because, you know, they liked, we were a rhythm section, and a pretty damn good one. So guys used to come and jam with us, but as far, oh yeah, well. Charlie Miller.

Charlie Miller, who's now living back in New Orleans, is a very, really excellent jazz trumpet player, classical trumpet player as well. And Jimmy Asenheimer, who was a really excellent clarinetist, played with the symphony, and was involved in, Buddy used to have an interesting term for the kind of music we were all kind of getting involved in. We were all getting interested in modern classical music as well. And most of us were studying composition. I had studied for a while with John Butler, who was kind of a…
That's an old tradition and not usually associated with modern jazz players.
